# probe


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Before kavacha builds an app or opens a window, it needs a few facts
about the machine it is on: whether a native window can be opened, which
installed Python py2app can build with, whether the app’s local server
has started, and whether a copy of the app is already running. This
module finds them out. None of its functions raise when the answer is
no. They return `None`, `False` or an empty list instead, so a caller
can print a clear message.

pywebview is the library that draws the native window. It uses a
different web engine on each platform and calls each one a GUI: `cocoa`
on macOS, `edgechromium` (Microsoft Edge WebView2) on Windows and `gtk`
on Linux. `BACKENDS` maps Python’s `sys.platform` names to these.
`FRAMEWORK_CANDIDATES` is used by
[`framework_python`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#framework_python),
further down.

[`backend`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#backend)
looks up the GUI for a platform, the current one by default, and returns
`None` for a platform pywebview does not support.
[`shell_ready`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#shell_ready)
checks the two things a window needs, a supported platform and an
installed pywebview, and returns `(True, gui)` or `(False, reason)`.
Call it before opening a window, so that a missing dependency produces a
readable message instead of an import error.

### py_version

``` python
def py_version(
    python
):
```

*The `(major, minor)` of `python`, or None when it will not say.*

py2app copies the Python interpreter into the bundle, and it can only do
that with a framework build. A framework build is the macOS layout that
python.org, Homebrew and Apple’s command line tools install, with the
interpreter inside a `Python.framework` folder. The interpreters uv and
pyenv download are python-build-standalone builds, which are laid out
differently and cannot be embedded.

[`is_framework`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#is_framework)
checks one interpreter by running it and asking. With no argument it
checks the Python running kavacha. When it checks another interpreter,
it also requires Python 3.12 or later.
[`py_version`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#py_version)
asks an interpreter for its `(major, minor)` version.
[`framework_python`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#framework_python)
goes through `FRAMEWORK_CANDIDATES`, the usual install paths, and
returns the first framework build it finds, or `None`. All three treat
an interpreter that is missing or will not run as a no, without raising.

The example uses three stand-in interpreters, small shell scripts that
answer the probe the way a real one would. The first is a framework
build of 3.13, which py2app can use. The second is a framework build of
3.11, which is too old. The third is a standalone 3.13, whose
`PYTHONFRAMEWORK` setting is empty, as it is for every interpreter uv
and pyenv install.

``` python
is_framework(fw), is_framework(old), is_framework(pbs)
```

    (True, False, False)

### wait_for_http

``` python
def wait_for_http(
    url, timeout:int=60, interval:float=0.1
):
```

*Wait until `url` answers with a success status or `timeout` seconds
pass, and return whether it did.*

An app’s window should not load its page until the local server is
listening, or the user sees a connection error.
[`wait_for_http`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#wait_for_http)
requests `url` every `interval` seconds until a request succeeds or
`timeout` seconds pass, and returns `True` or `False`. Here the server
has to answer with a success status, so a 404 counts as not ready.
`kavacha.window` has its own
[`wait_for_http`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#wait_for_http),
which accepts any HTTP response.

``` python
test_eq(wait_for_http(url), True)
test_eq(wait_for_http(url + 'missing', timeout=.3, interval=.05), False)
```

### running_from

``` python
def running_from(
    bundle, ps_output:NoneType=None
):
```

*PIDs of processes whose executable is inside `bundle`.*

Rebuilding an app while a copy of it is running breaks the running copy,
because the build replaces files it is still reading.
[`running_from`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#running_from)
lists the process IDs of programs whose executable is inside the folder
`bundle`. It reads the output of `ps`, or the text you pass as
`ps_output`, which is how the example runs without a real app. Only the
executable path counts, so a `grep` that mentions the bundle, or an app
in a folder with a similar name, does not match. The current process is
never listed, and if `ps` cannot run the result is an empty list.

``` python
ps = """  PID COMMAND
  101 /Apps/Demo.app/Contents/MacOS/Demo --serve
  102 /usr/bin/grep -r /Apps/Demo.app
  103 /Apps/Demo.app.old/Contents/MacOS/Demo
  104 /bin/zsh
"""
running_from('/Apps/Demo.app', ps)
```

    [101]
